part_title: Unstructured Features and Unsupervised Pattern Discovery
review_basis: Original numbered AIF Module 03 WebP slides 25–29 individually inspected in display order; narration follows actual labels, arrows, examples and decision cues.

scenes.title: Feature Engineering on Unstructured Data
scenes.narration: We have already seen how to prepare columns such as age or house size. But what if the input is a paragraph or a photograph? Follow this slide from left to right. The first box contains a customer review saying great product, really easy to use, and a landscape photograph. Their raw contents are unstructured. A traditional tabular learning algorithm cannot directly interpret a paragraph or the colors of every pixel as meaningful columns without an appropriate representation. The second box shows feature engineering. Text can be transformed into numerical features using methods such as T F I D F, which measures how informative a word is within documents, or word embeddings, which represent language patterns using vectors of numbers. For an image, a neural network such as a convolutional neural network can learn patterns related to edges, shapes, and textures. The third box shows blue and yellow feature vectors. A vector is simply an ordered list of numbers; these blocks are a picture of that idea, not real calculated values. Finally, the machine learning model uses the representations for a task, such as classifying the review as positive rather than negative. The illustrated prediction is positive, but that is not proof that every similarly worded review will be classified correctly. Notice the bottom decision cue: select features and processing suitable for the actual data type. Ask yourself: can we send raw photographs to a basic house-price spreadsheet model unchanged? Not meaningfully. We need a suitable image representation and a trained model for the intended task.

scenes.title: ML Algorithms – Unsupervised Learning
scenes.narration: Now we change learning style. In supervised learning each training example came with an answer. The heading here is unsupervised learning: discover structure without target labels. On the left, the visual shows one mixed collection of gray points entering an algorithm and emerging as three groups colored blue, gold, and green. The computer was not provided category names for those points; it searched for similarities in the data. This process is called clustering. The central column shows three related but different techniques. Clustering groups similar data points, association rule learning finds items or events that appear together, and anomaly detection flags observations that differ from typical patterns. Look at the shopping basket beside association rules: some customers buy coffee and a pastry together. That association can inform placement or promotions, but it does not prove one purchase caused the other. The anomaly picture shows one red dot away from blue points; unusual is not automatically bad. On the right, the customer segmentation example produces group A of frequent buyers, group B of price-sensitive shoppers, and group C of customers interested in new products. These are human interpretations attached after discovering patterns. The algorithm does not know that one customer is morally better or worse than another. We should check whether the groups actually help business decisions and whether the features introduce unfairness. The exam decision cue is clear: if you have no known outcomes and your goal is to explore structure, unsupervised learning is a likely fit. If you already have trusted spam and not-spam labels, supervised classification is more natural.

scenes.title: Clustering: customer segmentation
scenes.narration: This slide walks through clustering as a business workflow. First, on the far left, find the instruction to group similar customers. Similarity depends on measurable attributes, which we call features. The next panel suggests purchase frequency, product categories, and average order value. In the middle table, five illustrative customers buy different things. One frequently buys pizza, chips and drinks; another regularly buys baby-care products; another chooses fruit and vegetables; and others purchase sports gear or home goods occasionally. We feed these patterns to the clustering algorithm, represented by the gear labeled K means. K means is one example of a method that assigns items to a chosen number of groups based on their numerical characteristics. We must select and check a sensible number of clusters, rather than assuming three is always correct. Follow the colored arrows to the right. Group one is called convenience and snacks, group two family and baby care, and group three fresh and healthy. The colorful illustrations make the marketing interpretation tangible, but these are hypothetical customer personas and real purchases need not fit so neatly. We can then recommend relevant products or tailor promotions, while respecting privacy and avoiding unfair assumptions about individual shoppers. Clustering itself discovers groups; humans interpret whether a cluster represents something useful. A question to test yourself: if a store has no customer segment labels, but has purchase histories and wants to discover patterns, which method would you choose? Clustering. If its task were to predict an already labeled high-risk customer category, that would instead be supervised classification.

scenes.title: Association rules: finding co-occurring patterns
scenes.narration: The title asks us to find co-occurring patterns: items appearing together. Start with transaction receipts on the left. Each receipt records products bought in the same shopping visit, such as milk, bread, eggs, apples, or butter. These are records of what happened, not predictions or customer identities. In step two, the image illustrates an algorithm called Apriori. It identifies frequent itemsets, which are combinations of products that occur together often enough to analyze. The next box turns such patterns into association rules written in an if then style. One example says that if bread appears in a basket, butter is often present too. Another associates milk with eggs. Crucially, these rules describe observed relationships, not laws of nature: buying bread does not cause butter to appear, and the shop must evaluate how common and useful each pattern is. Step four shows bread and butter placed close together in a shop. A store might use a genuine association to improve product recommendations, shelf placement, or bundle offers. If the data is small or outdated, the apparent rule may mislead the business. That is why analysts may inspect measures such as support, the fraction of baskets containing an itemset, confidence, the fraction of relevant baskets satisfying the rule, and lift, which compares the association with what would be expected from ordinary purchasing rates. The bottom decision cue says to use association rule learning for transactional or event data when we want to uncover common combinations. Check the distinction: if our goal is to find what products are often bought together, use association rules; if we want to place shoppers into groups, use clustering.

scenes.title: Anomaly detection: spotting unusual events
scenes.narration: This visual follows a transaction through a fraud-review pipeline, but it makes an important distinction between unusual and proven fraudulent. On the far left, the transaction records include amount, location, time and other characteristics. The arrow leads to an anomaly detection model, with isolation forest shown as a specific example. An isolation forest tries to separate observations using randomized splits; observations that are easier to isolate can receive higher anomaly scores. The diagram then lists three illustrative normal transactions: a forty-two dollar online purchase, a sixty-seven dollar grocery purchase, and a three-hundred-ten-dollar travel booking. Beneath them, a fifteen-hundred-dollar transaction from a different country is highlighted as an anomaly. Its amount and location differ from the usual pattern in this teaching example. That does not mean the cardholder is committing fraud. Perhaps they are traveling or making an unusually large purchase. The right side therefore says flag for review and send for further investigation, rather than automatically declaring guilt. Read the bottom boxes from left to right: learn ordinary patterns, find unusual outliers, and send high-scoring cases for review. In a real system, analysts should examine false positives, meaning innocent activity flagged as suspicious, as well as false negatives, meaning truly problematic activity that went undetected. The decision cue asks when an event is rare or unexpected rather than simply which labeled category it belongs to. Quick check: would you immediately block every new country transaction? Not necessarily. A risk-based system should consider context, appropriate safeguards, and human review where needed.
